stem_md:
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM) is a global epidemic, affecting individuals in developing as well as developed countries.

**What will be the projected prevalence of diabetes in 2030, based on estimates by the International Diabetes Federation?**
explanation_md: According to the International Diabetes Federation statistics, 463 million people are currently afflicted by diabetes, and the numbers will rise to 578 million by 2030. Diabetes affects people of all ages, typically showing higher prevalence with increasing age up to 60–69 years. Four out of every five adults with undiagnosed diabetes live in low- and middle-income countries, where 87% of diabetes-related deaths occur.

stem_md:
A 53-year-old woman presented with symptoms of increased thirst, weight loss and an increased frequency of passing urine. She had a background medical history of bronchial asthma for which she occasionally used a salbutamol inhaler. On examination, her BMI was 29 kg/m². Her general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable except for central adiposity. Her fasting and random glucose readings were 6.5 and 9.2 mmol/L, respectively.

**Which one of the following biochemical cut-offs are diagnostic of diabetes, based on World Health Organization (WHO) criteria?**

options.A: 1-hour plasma glucose ≥11.1 on oral glucose tolerance test
options.B: Fasting glucose ≥6 mmol/L, with osmotic symptoms
options.C: Fasting glucose ≥7 mmol/L in an asymptomatic patient
options.D: Random glucose ≥8.5 mmol/L in an asymptomatic patient
options.E: Random glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L, with osmotic symptoms

explanation_md:
According to the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for the diagnosis of diabetes:

- A patient is diagnosed to have diabetes if he/she has osmotic symptoms, with biochemical evidence of random glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L; or fasting glucose ≥7 mmol/L; or 2-hour plasma glucose ≥11.1 on oral glucose tolerance test.
- An asymptomatic patient is diagnosed to have diabetes if he/she has biochemical evidence of fasting glucose ≥7 mmol/L or random glucose ≥11.1, with a second confirmatory plasma venous glucose measurement to be repeated on another day, with the glucose reading in the diabetic range (fasting, random, or 2-hour post-glucose tolerance test).
- In 2011, the WHO criteria added HbA1c as a diagnostic tool, with a cut-off of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) needed to diagnose diabetes.

stem_md:
HbA1c is a commonly used tool that is employed for the diagnosis of diabetes. Although it is highly specific for the diagnosis of diabetes, it is not particularly sensitive, with relatively more probability of obtaining a false negative test result.

**Which one of the following is an appropriate indication for the use of HbA1c for the diagnosis of diabetes?**
explanation_md:
HbA1c is not appropriate for use in the diagnosis of diabetes in the following situations:

- Patients on steroids or antipsychotics that can increase blood glucose readings
- Patients with acute pancreatic damage
- Pregnancy
- Patients suspected of having Type 1 DM
- Children and young adults
- Haemoglobinopathies, which can influence HbA1c results
- Patients with short duration of osmotic symptoms.

A 38-year-old man of Afro-Caribbean origin presented to the medical assessment unit with a 2-day history of feeling nauseous and generally unwell. He had a strong family history of diabetes. On examination, he had a BMI of 29 kg/m², with features of dehydration, a pulse rate of 104 beats/minute, and blood pressure of 90 mmHg systolic. His systemic examination was unremarkable.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Blood sugar | 28 mmol/L | |
| pH | 7.37 | 7.35–7.45 |
| HCO3 | 23 mmol/L | 22–27 |
| Na | 134 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 4.5 mmol/L | 3.5–4.5 |
| Amylase | 22 IU/L | <125 |
| Urine | Sugar +++, ketones 4+ | |

He was initially managed on a basis of insulin and intravenous fluids. He made a good clinical recovery and was discharged home with pre-mix insulin (70/30) injections bd. His subsequent blood tests show a negative anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibody status.

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate management approach for him when he is reviewed in a follow-up clinic visit in 4 weeks’ time?**
explanation_md: Ketosis-prone diabetes is more common in black and Hispanic ethnic subgroups. The patients are generally obese and may present with features of diabetic ketoacidosis. The autoimmune antibody status (anti-GAD antibodies) is generally negative. The management is initially on the lines of diabetic ketoacidosis (fluids/insulin/potassium replacement). Most of these patients can be managed on oral hypoglycaemic agents, with the discontinuation of insulin therapy within a few weeks to months.

stem_md:
A 32-year-old woman presented to her GP with osmotic symptoms (polydipsia and polyuria). She had a background history of sensorineural deafness, with a strong family history of diabetes (mother, maternal grandmother, and a few maternal cousins having Type 1 or Type 2). On examination, she had a BMI of 22 kg/m², with no clinical features of Cushing’s syndrome or hirsutism.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Blood sugar | 15.5 mmol/L | |
| pH | 7.37 | 7.35–7.45 |
| Venous HCO3 | 23 mmol/L | 22–27 |
| Sodium | 138 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| Potassium | 4.2 mmol/L | 3.5–4.5 |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy, based on her clinical profile?**
explanation_md: Mitochondrial diabetes is suspected in female patients with a strong familial clustering of diabetes, with predominantly maternal transmission of disease and the presence of sensorineural deafness. The degree and severity of insulinopenia is variable, with patients developing either Type 1 or Type 2 DM. The underlying defect in the majority of patients is the mitochondrial gene mutation (*A3243G*). The initial treatment of individuals with Type 2 DM presentation due to an underlying mitochondrial mutation can be with sulfonylureas. Metformin is contraindicated due to the risk of development of lactic acidosis. Hearing defects usually precede the development of diabetes in these patients.

stem_md: **Which one of the following specific membrane glucose transporters is present in the highest concentration in pancreatic beta cells?**
explanation_md: Specific membrane transporters are involved in the transport of glucose into the cells. There are two major categories of these membrane transporters—sodium-dependent and sodium-independent. The sodium-dependent transporters absorb glucose against its concentration gradient, while the sodium-independent transporters have an insulin-responsive isoform and further subdivide into Glut 1–7. Glut 2 is expressed in highest concentrations in pancreatic β cells, the basolateral membrane of the intestine, renal epithelial cells, and hepatocytes. Glut 4 is expressed in highest concentrations in insulin-sensitive tissue such as skeletal and cardiac muscle, with adipose tissue. Glut 5 is the only transporter that has higher specificity for fructose.

stem_md:
A 26-year-old Caucasian man with a background history of Type 1 DM is keen to know the risk of his offspring developing diabetes. His wife does not have diabetes or pre-diabetes.

**What is the risk of developing Type 1 DM for a baby born to a father with Type 1 DM?**
explanation_md:
The overall lifetime risk of developing Type 1 diabetes in a Caucasian population is currently 0.4%. The risk of developing Type 1 DM is around 1–2% for babies born to mothers with Type 1 DM (see Table 6.1). This risk increases to 3–6% if the father of the baby has Type 1 DM (and the mother does not have diabetes). The risk is 5–6 % if a sibling has Type 1 diabetes, while the concordance rate of developing Type 1 DM is ~50% in monozygotic twins.

**Table 6.1** Inheritance rate of Type 1 and Type 2 DM

| | Type 1 DM | Type 2 DM |
|---|---|---|
| Concordance rate in monozygotic twins | ~50% | 60–100 % |
| Mother with diabetes | 1–2% increased risk | ~25% |
| Father with diabetes | 3–6% increased risk | ~25% |

stem_md:
A 34-year-old woman presented to her primary care physician with osmotic symptoms such as polydipsia and polyuria. On examination, she had a BMI of 32 kg/m², with no phenotypic features of Cushing’s syndrome. Her fasting blood glucose readings were in the range of 8–9 mmol/L. She was keen to know the risk of the development of Type 2 DM in her twin sister.

**What is the concordance rate of developing Type 2 DM in monozygotic twins?**
explanation_md: The concordance rate of developing Type 2 DM in monozygotic twins is 60–100% as compared with a 30–35% concordance rate of developing Type 1 DM. This is indicative of a stronger genetic component to developing Type 2 DM as compared with Type 1 DM, although the human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-linked genes such as the *HLA-DR3-DQ2/DR4-DQ8* genotype are more strongly associated with the risk of developing later (20-fold increase of developing Type 1 DM as compared with the general population), rather than the former.

stem_md:
As part of a research trial, a healthy medical student was detected to have glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 (GAD65), insulin autoantibodies (IAA), and insulinoma-associated antigen-2 autoantibodies (IA-2A) in her blood.

**What is the probability of her developing Type 1 DM in the next 10 years on incidental detection of these three antibodies in her blood?**
explanation_md:
The presence of β cell autoantibodies is currently deemed as the earliest established sign of autoimmunity against the pancreatic islet β cells. Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65), insulin autoantibodies (IAA), insulinoma-associated antigen-2 autoantibodies (IA-2A), and zinc transporter 8 autoantibodies (ZnT8A) are the primary antibodies against islet cells.

- Islet cell antibodies are rarely detected before the age of 6 months.
- Peak incidence for appearance of IAA2 and GAD antibodies is 9–24 months and 36 months respectively.
- 70% of Type 1 DM patients have three or four antibodies, while in 10% at least one autoantibody is present.
- Presence of IA2 and ZnT8 is associated with relatively rapid progression to Type 1 DM.
- The presence of three out of four autoantibodies in the blood of a patient without diabetes increases the 10-year risk of development of Type 1 DM to 80–90%.

stem_md:
A 40-year-old schoolteacher presented to the medical assessment unit with a 2-month history of osmotic symptoms and elevated blood glucose levels. There was no family history of diabetes and she was not on any medication. On examination, her BMI was 22 kg/m², with normal general physical and systemic examination.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Random blood sugar | 16.5 mmol/L | |
| pH | 7.40 | 7.35–7.45 |
| HCO3 | 25 mmol/L | 22–27 |
| Na | 140 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 3.7 mmol/L | 3.5–4.5 |
| Urine | Sugar ++; ketones negative | |

**Which one of the following tests may be useful in establishing the underlying diagnosis, considering her clinical profile?**

options.D: Serum ferritin and total iron-binding capacity

explanation_md: Latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood is a subtype of diabetes in which patients may present with phenotypic features of Type 2 DM, while displaying the presence of markers of autoimmunity (anti-GAD antibodies). Most of these patients are in the age group of 30–50 years, may or may not have a normal BMI (obesity can be a confounding factor), and may present with elevated blood glucose levels, with osmotic symptoms. These patients can be managed initially with oral hypoglycaemic agents, although the β-cell function may decline over months to a few years, necessitating a relatively early requirement for insulin use.

stem_md:
A neonate aged 6 weeks presented to the paediatric emergency unit with failure to thrive and dehydration. His blood tests showed elevated blood glucose levels with low serum bicarbonate and elevated ketones, consistent with a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis.

**Which one of the following genetic mutations is associated with development of neonatal diabetes?**

options.E: Potassium β cell K ATP channel (KCNJ11 and ABCC8)

explanation_md:
Neonatal diabetes usually develops within the first 6 months of birth and is associated with gene mutations such as *KCNJ11* and *ABCC8* (encoding for KIR 6.2 and SUR1 subunit of pancreatic K-ATP channel involved in insulin secretion). Treatment is with insulin and a high caloric intake initially, although the patients may be responsive to sulfonylurea therapy and a switch to sulfonylureas should be considered once clinically stable.

The following features help to distinguish monogenetic diabetes from Type 1 DM in children:

- Onset within 6 months of birth (*KCNJ11* or *ABCC8* mutation)
- Milder hyperglycaemia (glucokinase mutation)
- Asymptomatic hyperglycaemia.

stem_md:
A 29-year-old woman was referred to the antenatal clinic as she had been labelled as having gestational diabetes (GDM) during her previous pregnancy. She had a family history of Type 2 DM (mother). On examination, her BMI was 23 kg/m². An oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) carried out during the first trimester showed the following results: 0-minutes blood glucose 5.8 mmol/L; 2-hour blood glucose 8.9 mmol/L.

In her previous pregnancy, she had been treated with basal insulin to control her fasting hyperglycaemia. She had not required insulin during the post-partum period.

**Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based on her clinical profile?**
explanation_md:
Glucokinase (GCK) mutation is associated with altered glucose sensing in the pancreatic β-cells, leading to mild hyperglycaemia with elevated fasting blood glucose readings (typically 5.5–8 mmol/L). Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) due to GCK mutation is usually asymptomatic; treatment is not needed and there is no risk of any diabetes complications, hence no need for the usual diabetes screening. However, if GCK MODY is confirmed in the mother, insulin might be considered to prevent foetal macrosomia (this can be considered in foetuses with a rising abdominal circumference >70th centile). As it can be difficult to distinguish it from gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), the following clinical criteria can increase the rate of detection for GCK-MODY:

1. Persisting fasting hyperglycaemia (5.5–8 mmol/L)
2. A small 2-hour increment (<4.6mmol/L) during OGTT, in or outside pregnancy (in contrast, patients with GDM often have normal fasting plasma glucose with a relatively larger plasma glucose increment at 2 hours on OGTT)
3. Fasting glucose intolerance diagnosed in the first trimester
4. Slim rather than overweight or obese, although obesity does not exclude the diagnosis
5. Previous insulin treatment used during pregnancy (usually in an attempt to lower fasting glucose) but, post-delivery, controlled on diet
6. History of GDM or fasting hyperglycaemia (>5.5mmol/L) or Type 2 DM in a first-degree relative

Further information on the management of pregnancy in patients with hyperglycaemia due to disease-causing variants in the glucokinase (*GCK*) gene can be found at the DiabeticGenes website. https://www.diabetesgenes.org/what-is-mody/what-is-glucokinase-gck/

stem_md:
A 25-year-old man was incidentally detected to have elevated fasting as well as post-prandial blood glucose readings on routine blood tests. He had a background medical history of a renal cyst, which had been managed conservatively. He also had a strong family history of diabetes, with some of his first cousins, uncles, and grandparents having diabetes requiring medications or insulin. On examination, he had a BMI of 21 kg/m², with no peripheral stigmata of insulin resistance, such as acanthosis nigricans.

**Which one of the following genetic mutations is most likely, based on his clinical profile?**
explanation_md:
Monogenic diabetes usually affects 1–2% of individuals with diabetes, although most cases remain unrecognized. The characteristics of monogenic diabetes include a diagnosis before the fourth decade of age, a strong family history of diabetes, and absence of surrogate markers of insulin resistance (lack of central obesity, acanthosis nigricans, dyslipidaemia).

HNF-1B mutation is characterized by an association with genitourinary malformations, such as renal cysts and uterine abnormalities.

Table 6.2 summarizes the characteristic features of various subtypes of monogenic diabetes.

**Table 6.2** Characteristic features of various subtypes of monogenic diabetes

| Name | Previous name | Prevalence (% of total patients with monogenic diabetes) | Clinical features |
|---|---|---|---|
| *HNF-4A* | MODY 1 | 5–10% | Progressive cell decline, neonatal hyperinsulinaemia, and hypoglycaemia; responsive to sulfonylureas |
| Glucokinase MODY | MODY 2 | 30–70% | No risk of development of microvascular complications; mild fasting hyperglycaemia (5.5–8 mmol/L), HbA1c remains stable over life (HbA1c <64 mmol/L) |
| *HNF-1A MODY* | MODY 3 | 30–70% | Associated with progressive decline in B-cell function and risk of microvascular complications; marked sensitivity to sulfonylureas therapy |
| *IPF1* | MODY 4 | <1% | Onset after age >35 years; pancreatic agenesis in homozygotes |
| *HNF1B MODY* | MODY5 | 5–10% | Associated with renal cysts and genitourinary tract malformations |
| *KCNJ11* ABCC8 | | <1% | Present with high blood glucose values during first 6 months of life; responsive to sulfonylureas |

stem_md:
A 24-year-old woman was reviewed in the diabetes clinic on a routine follow-up visit. She had been diagnosed as having Type 1 DM aged 16 years, when she was noted to have had elevated fasting blood glucose levels on routine blood tests, while undergoing treatment for a urinary tract infection. She had been on a basal-bolus insulin regimen, with a total insulin requirement of 10–12 units/day. She had good glycaemic control, as reflected by HbA1c of 46–50 mmol/mol over the previous 8 years. On examination, she had a BMI of 24 kg/m², with no evidence of diabetic retinopathy or peripheral neuropathy.

**Which one of the following characteristic features should raise the clinical suspicion of MODY in this patient?**
explanation_md:
The following laboratory or clinical characteristics should raise the clinical suspicion of MODY in patients labelled as Type 1 DM after 3–5 years of diagnosis:

- Persistent urinary c peptides detection (even if insulin treated)
- Low insulin dose requirement
- No tendency to develop diabetic ketoacidosis
- Absence of anti-GAD and islet cell antigens (ICAs)
- Strong family history of diabetes
- Marked sensitivity to sulfonylureas

stem_md:
A 40-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with symptoms of polydipsia and polyuria for the previous 6 weeks. He had a strong family history of diabetes, with both his parents and an elder brother on oral hypoglycaemic agents or insulin for blood glucose control. On examination, he had a BMI of 24 kg/m², with the presence of dark hyperpigmented skin in the armpit, although there was no evidence of diabetic retinopathy or peripheral neuropathy.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Random blood sugar | 14.2 mmol/L | |
| pH | 7.43 | 7.35–7.45 |
| Venous HCO3 | 24 mmol/L | 22–27 |
| Na | 135 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 3.5 mmol/L | 3.5–4.5 |
| Urine | Sugar ++, ketones negative | |

**Which one of the following clinical/biochemical features will support the diagnosis of Type 2 DM (over a diagnosis of monogenic diabetes) in this man?**
explanation_md:
The following clinical characteristics should raise the clinical suspicion of MODY in patients labelled as Type 2 DM:

- Younger age of onset (<45 years, frequently at younger age)
- Normal BMI
- Strong family history of diabetes
- Fasting hyperglycaemia with no or mildly elevated post-prandial glucose (glucokinase mutation)
- Renal cysts, genitourinary tract abnormalities (HNF-1B mutation)
- Absence of surrogate markers of insulin resistance, such as acanthosis nigricans, central obesity, dyslipidaemia, hypertension
- Marked sensitivity to sulfonylurea therapy (HNF-1A or HNF-4A mutation)

stem_md:
A 55-year-old man was reviewed in the diabetes clinic on an annual follow-up visit. He had a background history of Type 2 DM for 8 years, and was taking metformin and gliclazide therapy. On examination, he had features of bilateral neuropathy.

**Which one of the following side effects is associated with long-term metformin use?**
explanation_md: Metformin is the most commonly used first-line medication for the management of Type 2 DM. Its use has been linked with malabsorption of vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor from ileum, which can lead to peripheral neuropathy, mental changes, and macrocytic anaemia. The B12 deficiency with metformin is progressive and routine assessment of B12 levels should be considered in patients on long-term metformin therapy.

stem_md:
A 66-year-old woman with Type 2 DM for the previous 15 years presented to her primary care physician with symptoms of fatigue and weight loss. She was on metformin and sitagliptin therapy for her diabetes. On examination, she had pallor, with evidence of background diabetic retinopathy.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Hb | 12.8 g/L | 12–15 |
| Na | 140 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 4.5 mmol/L | 3.5–5.5 |
| Urea | 28.2 mg/dL | 7–20 |
| Creatinine | 135 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| eGFR | 42 mL/minute/1.73 m² | |
| HbA1c | 55 mmol/mol | <46 |

**According to NICE guidelines, which one of the following is the correct indication to stop metformin therapy in the presence of renal impairment?**
explanation_md: According to the NICE guidelines (NG28), metformin dose needs to be reviewed if eGFR <45 mL/minute/1.73 m². Metformin therapy should be stopped if eGFR <30 mL/minute/1.73 m².

stem_md:
Dipeptidyl peptidase inhibitors 4 (DPP4) inhibit the enzyme DPP4 and prevent breakdown of endogenous incretins.

**Which one of the following DPP4 inhibitors is excreted unchanged in faeces and does not require any dose modification in renal disease?**
explanation_md: Linagliptin is a DPP4 inhibitor that is predominantly excreted unchanged in faeces, with metabolism of the drug playing a minor role in overall pharmacokinetics. It is a weak inhibitor of cytochrome P450. There is no dose adjustment required for linagliptin in renal-failure patients.

stem_md:
Pioglitazone can be used as a second- or third-line therapy when glycaemic control remains poor, especially in the presence of a significant degree of insulin resistance, although the use of this agent has been associated with complications such as fluid retention.

**Which of the following side effects/complications is associated with Pioglitazone use?**
explanation_md:
Pioglitazone and rosiglitazone are thiazolidinedione compounds, which act as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ-agonists and help reduce peripheral insulin resistance. Weight gain of 2–3 kg is relatively common with pioglitazone use and is dose related. Pioglitazone use is also associated with the risk of fluid retention due to peripheral vasodilation and renal sodium retention. In the PROactive trial, Pioglitazone use was associated with a non-significant increase in the number of patients who developed bladder carcinoma. There are case reports linking the development of macular oedema with the use of pioglitazone therapy. This agent has also been associated with an increased risk of fractures (mostly in distal long bones of post-menopausal women).

Rosiglitazone use was also associated with increased cardiovascular risks and it was withdrawn from the market in 2010, following a review by the European Medicines Agency.

stem_md:
Statins are the commonest agents used to manage dyslipidaemia in patients with diabetes, although these have been associated with an increased statistical risk of development of diabetes.

**Which one of the following statins has been associated with a reduction in risk of development of Type 2 DM?**
explanation_md:
Statin use has been linked with an increased risk of the development of diabetes. A meta-analysis of five trials (PROVE-IT, A to Z, TNT, IDEAL, and SEARCH), involving more than 32,000 patients without diabetes, compared the effects of high-dose statins with conventional dose statins, with a 12% increased risk of developing diabetes in the former compared with the latter.

In another meta-analysis of 13 statin trials, 4,278 participants out of a total of 91,140 developed diabetes during a mean period of 4 years, equating to a 9% increased risk for development of diabetes while on statin therapy. Statin use was observed to be associated with an increased risk of development of Type 2 DM with pooled Hazard ratio (HR) (95% CI) for incident diabetes of 1.36 (1.17 to 1.58) in the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) outcome study.

Alternatively, the subgroup analysis results of the LIVES (Livalo Effectiveness and Safety) trial have shown improvement in glucose homeostasis, with an increase in HDL-cholesterol levels with pitavastatin use.

stem_md:
Statin therapy is the mainstay of treatment for patients with familial (homozygous or heterozygous) hypercholesterolaemia.

**Which one of the following biological changes is associated with use of statin therapy?**
explanation_md: Statins have been the mainstay therapy to lower LDL cholesterol levels in patients with both homozygous, as well as heterozygous hypercholesterolaemia, with efficacy ranging from 15% to 53%, based on the agent and dose used. These agents act by inhibiting the hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase enzyme. Statins also lead to an up-regulation of both the LDL-receptor, as well as proprotein convertase substilisin kexin 9 (PCKS9) expression. PCSK9 is a key regulator of LDL-C levels as it promotes lysosomal-mediated degradation of the LDL-receptor. The up-regulation of PCSK9 expression significantly attenuates the LDL-C lowering potential of statins.

stem_md:
Corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone, prednisolone) and antipsychotic medications (e.g. olanzapine, risperidone) are commonly prescribed medications which are associated with weight gain and impaired glycaemic control.

**Which of the following medications has also been observed to have an adverse impact on glycaemic control?**
explanation_md: High-dose statin use has been associated with an increased risk of development of diabetes. The use of corticosteroids is associated with increased insulin resistance, decreased glucose uptake in muscle, and increased gluconeogenesis. Nicotinic acid use has been linked with worsening of glycaemic control, secondary to increased gluconeogenesis. Protease inhibitors that are used as part of anti-retroviral therapy have been shown to induce insulin resistance by inhibition of the GLUT4 transporter. Atypical antipsychotics, such as olanzapine and clozapine, have been associated with an increased risk of diabetes. mTOR inhibitors and everolimus use have been associated with 5.3% incidence of high-grade hyperglycaemia.

stem_md:
A 55-year-old man with a background history of Type 2 DM was referred to the diabetes clinic in view of his suboptimal glycaemic control, despite being on metformin and gliclazide therapy. His past medical history included osteoarthritis, dyslipidaemia, and hypertension. On examination, he had a BMI of 35 kg/m², with evidence of pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. He was considered for initiation of therapy with glucagon-like peptide receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) in view of his suboptimal glycaemic control.

**Which one of the following is a correct statement regarding GLP-1 analogue therapy use?**

options.A: GLP1-RA are contraindicated if eGFR<45 mL/minute/1.73 m²
options.B: GLP1 RA should be avoided in patients with background retinopathy
options.C: GLP1-RA should be discontinued if <1% drop of HbA1c at 6 months
options.D: GLP1-RA should be discontinued if <5% body weight loss at 6 months
options.E: GLP1-RA should not be combined with insulin therapy

explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines, GLP1-RA can be considered if glycaemic control remains suboptimal despite using triple therapy (metformin, a DDP-4 inhibitor, and a sulfonylurea; or metformin, pioglitazone, and a sulfonylurea) and for patients who have:

- a BMI ≥35kg/m² (adjust accordingly for people from black, Asian, and other minority ethnic groups) and specific psychological or other medical problems associated with obesity; or
- a BMI <35kg/m² and for whom:
  - insulin therapy would have significant occupational implications or
  - weight loss would benefit other significant obesity-related comorbidities.

According to NICE guidelines, treatment with GLP1-RA needs to be continued only if the person with Type 2 DM has had a beneficial metabolic response (i.e. a reduction of at least 11 mmol/mol [1.0%] in HbA1c and a weight loss of at least 3% of initial body weight in 6 months). GLP-1RA (such as liraglutide, semaglutide, and dulaglutide) can be administered up to an eGFR of 15 mL/min/1.73 m², although these need to be avoided in end-stage renal disease.

Multicentric randomized controlled trials such as LEADER (liraglutide), SUSTAIN 6 (semaglutide), and REWIND (dulaglutide) have shown a trend in reducing incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). As a result, the current EASD/ADA consensus supports use of GLP1-RA at an earlier stage for the patients with Type 2 DM.

The main side effects of GLP-1 analogue therapy are gastrointestinal disturbance, including nausea and vomiting, diarrhoea, and abdominal pain. There is no conclusive evidence related to an increased risk of acute pancreatitis with these agents.

stem_md:
Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have been approved for use in the management of patients with Type 2 DM.

**Which one of the following is a known side effect with use of SGLT2 inhibitors?**
explanation_md:
SGLT2 inhibitor use is associated with the increased risk of development of urinary tract and genital infections. The FDA adverse event reporting system noted use of SGLT2 inhibitors being associated with ~7-fold increase in developing acidosis. Out of a total of 192 patients reported to have ketoacidosis, 71% had euglycaemic ketoacidosis.

An SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin) can be considered as an option for treating adult patients with Type 1 diabetes, in addition to insulin, if their BMI is at least 27 kg/m² and when insulin alone does not provide adequate glycaemic control despite optimal insulin therapy, only if:

- They are on insulin doses of more than 0.5 units/kg of body weight per day **and**
- They have completed a structured education programme that is evidence-based, quality-assured, and delivered by trained educators, and includes information about diabetic ketoacidosis on such matters as:
  - How to recognize its risk factors, signs, and symptoms
  - How and when to monitor blood ketone levels
  - What actions to take for elevated blood ketones

  **and**
- Treatment is started and supervised by a consultant physician specializing in endocrinology and diabetes.

stem_md:
Gluconeogenesis is a process of generation of glucose from non-glucose sources such as amino-acids, glycerol, fatty acids, and lactate.

**Which one of the following organs participates in the process of gluconeogenesis in human beings?**
explanation_md: The liver and kidneys are the primary organs participating in the process of gluconeogenesis in human beings.

stem_md:
A 55-year-old man was reviewed in the diabetes clinic on an annual follow-up visit. He had a background history of Type 2 DM (diagnosed 5 years previously), morbid obesity, and dyslipidaemia. He was a non-smoker with an alcohol intake of about 3–4 units/week. On examination, he had central obesity with a BMI of 42 kg/m². His hepatitis screen, iron studies, and autoimmune screen were normal. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed a fatty liver with a normal gall bladder and bile duct.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Albumin | 34 g/L | 30–50 |
| ALP | 255 U/L | 50–125 |
| ALT | 82 mU/L | 05–58 |
| Bilirubin | 1.2 mg/L | 0.1–1 |
| HbA1c | 95 mmol/mol | <46 |

Based on his clinical profile, together with the results of biochemical and radiological tests, a diagnosis of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) secondary to diabetes/metabolic syndrome was considered.

**Which one of the following is the cornerstone of management of patients with NAFLD?**
explanation_md:
Type 2 diabetes is associated with a whole spectrum of liver diseases, including abnormal liver function tests, non-alcoholic hepatosteatosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. According to the Verona diabetes study, cirrhosis was the fourth leading cause of death in patients with diabetes. Diabetes is also emerging as one of the commonest aetiologies of patients otherwise labelled with cryptogenic cirrhosis. Patients with poorly controlled diabetes characteristically have elevated triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, elevated LDL-cholesterol levels, with varying degrees of insulin resistance. There is increased lipolysis resulting in elevated levels of free fatty acids and overloading of the hepatic mitochondrial β-oxidation system. Free fatty acids induce the production of oxygen-free radicals and generation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α, and interleukin-1 and 6, leading to cellular damage.

Lifestyle measures remain the cornerstone of management of patients with NAFLD. There is evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) supporting the use of pioglitazone, leading to a reduction in steatohepatitis and a modest effect on fibrosis. DPP4 inhibitors have not been associated with any significant benefit for management of patients with NAFLD, although emerging evidence with use of GLP1 RA (liraglutide) in patients with NAFLD seems promising.

**Which one of the following is the probable diagnosis, based on his clinical profile?**
explanation_md:
Haemochromatosis (bronze diabetes) is a hereditary (*HFE/SCL11A3/HAMP* gene mutations) or acquired (e.g. secondary to repeated blood transfusions) disorder, which leads to excessive iron accumulation in various tissues and organs, such as the pancreas, liver, and heart, and in joints. Patients can present with non-specific symptoms such as fatigue and malaise, low libido, arthritis, late-onset diabetes, liver disorders, bronzed skin, and cardiomyopathy.

Patients with haemochromatosis have an increased transferrin saturation (normal <30%), with elevated ferritin levels (it may be normal in early disease). Liver biopsy and genetic tests are helpful to establish the diagnosis.

A 33-year-old Caucasian woman was reviewed during a routine antenatal check-up when she was 16 weeks pregnant. It was her second pregnancy, with the birthweight of her first baby being 4.1 kg. She had a family history of Type 1 DM (grandmother). On examination, her BMI was 26.5 kg/m².

**According to NICE guidelines for the management of diabetes in pregnancy, the presence of which of the following factors should act as a trigger to screen for GDM?**
explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines, the following have been shown as independent risk factors for development of GDM and, thus, the presence of any of the following should trigger screening for GDM:

- BMI >30 kg/m²
- Family history of Type 2 diabetes (first-degree relatives)
- Previous GDM
- Previous macrosomic baby (weighing >4.5 kg)
- South East Asian, Black Caribbean, or Middle Eastern ethnic origin

stem_md:
A 35-year-old woman with Type 1 DM was reviewed in the diabetes clinic on a routine visit. She was on a basal-bolus insulin regimen, with good glycaemic control as evidenced by a HbA1c value of 48 mmol/mol. She was keen to start a family and sought preconception advice. She was known to have hypertension and was on amlodipine tablets. She had no microalbuminuria. An estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 57 mL/minute/m². Her last retinal assessment had been carried out 8 months before.

**According to NICE guidelines, which of the following is correct advice regarding management of patients with diabetes in the preconception period?**

options.C: Renal referral as eGFR <60 mL/minute/1.73 m²
options.D: Retinal assessment as last one carried out >6 months ago
options.E: Target pre-meal plasma glucose reading of 5–8 mmol/mol

explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines for the management of diabetes in pregnancy (NG3), preconception care and assessment of patients with diabetes should include:

- Folic acid supplement (5 mg/day) until week 12 of pregnancy
- Self-monitoring of blood glucose
- Ketone testing strips to women with Type 1 DM
- Offer of up to monthly HbA1c
- Retinal assessment, if not done in the previous 6 months
- Renal assessment and consideration for referral to renal physician if:
  - eGFR <45 mL/minute/1.73 m², or
  - Serum creatinine is 120 mmol/L or more, or
  - Urinary albumin to creatinine ratio is greater than 30 mg/mmol
- Strong advice to avoid pregnancy if HbA1c >86 mmol/mol (10%)
- Stop statins, angiotensin-II receptor antagonists, and ACE inhibitors before pregnancy or as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
- Target fasting plasma glucose readings of 5–7 mmol/L on waking up and 4–7 mmol/L before meals at other times of the day

stem_md:
A 24-year-old woman with Type 1 DM, diagnosed 6 years previously, was reviewed during a routine follow-up visit to the antenatal clinic. She was taking a basal-bolus insulin regimen and had suboptimal preconception glycaemic control as reflected by a HbA1c of 62 mmol/mol. She was keen to assess the risk of congenital malformation in her offspring.

**What is the relative risk of developing congenital malformations in children born to mothers with diabetes compared with the non-diabetic population?**
explanation_md: There is a 2–4-fold risk of developing major congenital malformations in children born to mothers with Type 1 DM compared with the non-diabetic population. The commonest congenital malformations include cardiac, renal, and neural tube defects.

stem_md:
A 25-year-old schoolteacher with Type 1 DM attended her first joint antenatal–diabetes clinic while she was 10 weeks pregnant. She had been diagnosed with Type 1 DM when she was 14 years old and remained well controlled on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Her preconception HbA1c level was 49 mmol/mol. Her last retinal screening had been carried out 6 months before. Her renal function was within the normal range and she had no microalbuminuria.

**Which of the following is correct advice, based on NICE guidelines, for the management of women with diabetes in pregnancy?**

options.A: Advise fasting and 2-hour post-meal blood glucose monitoring
options.B: Ketone testing not recommended due to high false positive rate
options.C: Measure eGFR to assess renal function
options.D: Retinal screening at baseline and at 28 weeks
options.E: Soluble insulin preferable over rapid-acting insulin (e.g. aspart)

explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines on antenatal care for women with Type 1 DM:

- Check fasting, pre-meal, 1-hour post-meal, and bedtime blood glucose
- Measure baseline HbA1c at booking appointment
- Consider rapid-acting analogues such as aspart and lispro (advantageous as compared to soluble insulin)
- Offer continuous glucose monitoring in pregnancy (if not already using it)
- Offer blood ketone testing strips and a meter
- Offer retinal assessment by digital imaging with mydriasis, using tropicamide, following their first antenatal clinic appointment (unless they have had a retinal assessment in the previous 3 months), and again at 28 weeks
- If diabetic retinopathy (DR) is present at booking, offer an additional retinal assessment at 16–20 weeks; presence of DR is not a contraindication for rapid optimization of glycaemic control
- Offer renal assessment at baseline; eGFR should not be used to measure renal function

stem_md:
A 32-year-old woman with Type 1 DM was reviewed in the joint antenatal–diabetes clinic. She was on a basal-bolus insulin regimen, with satisfactory glycaemic control (HbA1c 48 mmol/mol, preconception).

**According to NICE guidelines, which one of the following statements is correct with regards to blood glucose monitoring and target blood glucose values?**

options.A: Aim for fasting blood glucose ≤6 mmol/L
options.D: Aim to maintain capillary glucose reading ≥4.5 mmol/L

explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines for the management of diabetes in pregnancy, women with Type 1 DM and/or women with any type of diabetes using multiple daily insulin are advised to measure fasting, pre-meal,1-hour post-meal, and bedtime blood glucose levels (around eight times/day). Women with Type 2 DM and GDM who are treated with either diet, oral anti-diabetic agents, or single-dose intermediate-acting or long-acting insulin are advised to measure their glucose levels at fasting and 1-hour post-meal (around four times/day).

The blood glucose target in pregnancy needs to be individualized, with the following targets (if achievable without increasing the risk of problematic hypoglycaemia):

- Fasting blood glucose level <3 mmol/L
- 1-hour post-prandial glucose level <7.8 mmol/L
- 2-hour post-prandial glucose level <6.4 mmol/L
- Maintain capillary blood glucose levels >4 mmol/L

stem_md:
A 37-year-old woman with Type 2 DM was reviewed in the diabetes clinic on a routine follow-up visit. She was on metformin (1 g twice a day) and glargine insulin (lantus, 8 units at night-time) therapy, with good glycaemic control as reflected by a HbA1c of 50 mmol/mol. She was also on ramipril (5 mg once a day) for blood pressure control. She had a family history of mixed dyslipidaemia. She was keen to start a family and was seeking preconception advice.

**According to NICE guidelines, which one of the following is the correct statement regarding her further management during pregnancy?**
explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines:

- Metformin use is safe during pregnancy.
- Isophane insulin is the first choice for long-acting insulin during pregnancy.
- Available evidence does not suggest adverse effects of short-acting insulin analogues (aspart and lispro insulin) during pregnancy.
- Long-acting insulin analogues (detemir and glargine) can be continued in women with Type 2 DM who had good glycaemic control before pregnancy.
- Statins and ACE inhibitor therapy need to be stopped during the antenatal period.
- Women with an HbA1c >86 mmol/mol (10%) should be advised against pregnancy given the risks associated with high HbA1c such as miscarriage, stillbirth, congenital malformation, and neonatal death.

A 36-year-old woman with Type 2 DM was reviewed on a routine follow-up visit to the diabetes clinic. She was planning to start a family and was keen to assess the risk of development of congenital malformations and perinatal mortality in her offspring.

**Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the risk of perinatal mortality and congenital malformations in the offspring of women with Type 2 DM, compared with women with Type 1 DM?**
explanation_md: There is four-fold increased perinatal mortality in children born to mothers with diabetes, compared with the non-diabetic population. There is no conclusive evidence of differences in perinatal mortality and congenital malformation risk in the offspring of women with Type 1 or Type 2 DM.

stem_md: **Which one of the following is the correct diagnostic criterion for the diagnosis of GDM for the 75 g OGTT (based on NICE NG3 guidelines)?**
explanation_md: GDM is diagnosed based on 75-g OGTT when fasting glucose is >5.6 mmol/L and/or 2-hour post-test glucose is >7.8 mmol/L.

A 45-year-old man of Afro-Caribbean origin was reviewed in the diabetes clinic on a routine follow-up visit. He had a background history of Type 2 DM, hypertension, and sickle cell disease. He was on isophane insulin (12 units twice a day) and metformin sustained-release tablets (2 g once a day). His home blood glucose monitoring readings were variable, with a range of 10–15 mmol/L throughout the day. He had not suffered from any hypoglycaemic episodes in recent months.

**Which one of the following is relatively the most accurate parameter to assess his glycaemic control?**
explanation_md:
HbA1c measurement is the standard laboratory test for the assessment of glycaemic control. Clinical conditions which reduce haemoglobin lifespan and haemoglobinopathies can impact the reliability of HbA1c results (falsely low readings). In contrast, falsely elevated HbA1c values can be seen in uraemia (carbamylated Hb) or in the presence of HbF.

The man in this scenario had suboptimal glycaemic control, as reflected by his elevated home blood sugar readings, although his HbA1c was low (falsely low due to underlying sickle cell disease). As a result, his insulin dose needs to be increased to improve glycaemic control.

In patients with haemoglobinopathies, measurement of fructosamine may provide a better assessment of glycaemic control compared with HbA1c. Fructosamine measurement is dependent on serum protein glycation and remains unaffected by the presence of haemoglobinopathies. In contrast to HbA1c, fructosamine measurement provides assessment of blood glucose levels during the preceding 2–3 weeks only.

| Triglycerides | 12 mmol/L | |
| LDL cholesterol | 4.1 mmol/L | |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step for the further management of his elevated triglyceride levels?**
explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines:

- In individuals with triglyceride concentration >20 mmol/L (after excluding poor glycaemic control and excess alcohol intake), seek urgent specialist advice.
- If the triglyceride levels are 10–20 mmol/L, repeat the triglyceride measurement with a fasting test (after an interval of 5 days, but within 2 weeks) and review for potential secondary causes of dyslipidaemia (such as excessive alcohol intake, metabolic syndrome, poor diabetes control, and drugs). Specialist advice is needed if the repeat fasting triglyceride concentration remains >10 mmol/L.
- In individuals with triglyceride levels of 4.5–9.9 mmol/L, the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) might be underestimated by risk assessment tools.
- In patients with mixed dyslipidaemia (fasting total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L and triglycerides level >4.5 mmol/L), exclude the presence of remnant hyperlipidaemia by measuring the ratio of high-density lipoprotein/apolipoprotein B with subsequent fasting beta-quantification, if the ratio is raised.

A 62-year-old retired schoolteacher attended the diabetes clinic on a routine follow-up visit. He had a background history of hypertension and Type 2 DM for 20 years. He felt frustrated about his inability to lose weight despite his best possible efforts. He was currently taking metformin (1 g twice daily), liraglutide (1.2 mg subcutaneously once daily), ramipril 10 mg once daily, and amlodipine (10 mg once a day). On examination, his BMI was 38 kg/m². His blood pressure was 152/92 mm of Hg.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |

| HbA1c | 89 mmol/mol | |

**According to NICE guidelines for obesity (CG189), the presence of which of the following criteria would deem him as a suitable candidate for bariatric surgery?**

options.C: BMI >35 Kg/m² and high blood pressure
options.D: BMI >35 Kg/ m² and inability to lose weight

explanation_md:
According to the NICE guidelines for obesity, bariatric surgery is a treatment option for people with obesity if all of the following criteria are fulfilled:

- BMI >40 kg/m² or BMI 35–40 kg/ m² and other significant disease (e.g. hypertension and diabetes in this scenario) which could be improved with weight loss
- All appropriate non-surgical measures have been tried
- Patient is fit for surgery and commits to long-term follow-up
- Patient has been receiving (or would receive) intensive management in a tier 3 weight management service

A 55-year-old man with Type 2 DM for 15 years was reviewed in the diabetes clinic on a routine follow-up visit. He was taking metformin, gliclazide, and ramipril tablets. On examination, he had a BMI of 27 kg/m². His blood pressure was 145/90 mmHg. Retinal examination showed evidence of background diabetic retinopathy.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Urinary albumin creatinine ratio | < 3mg/mmol | |
| Urinary microscopy | Normal | |
| eGFR creatinine | 52 ml/min/1.73m² (unchanged eGFR as compared to previous clinic visit 6 months before) | |

**Which one of the following can be used to confirm or rule out chronic kidney disease (CKD) in this patient?**
explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines, eGFR cystatinC can be considered at initial diagnosis to confirm or rule out chronic kidney disease (CKD) in people with:

- An eGFR creatinine of 45–59 ml/min/1.73 m² (sustained for at least 90 days)
- No proteinuria (urinary ACR<3 mg/mmol) and without any other marker of kidney disease

stem_md:
A 62-year-old woman with Type 2 DM for over 20 years was reviewed in the diabetes clinic on a routine follow-up visit. She was on metformin, dapagliflozin, and sitagliptin tablets for Type 2 DM. She was taking lisinopril and amlodipine tablets for blood pressure (BP) control. On examination, she had a BMI of 30.5 kg/m². Her BP was 142/84 mmHg. She had clinical evidence of peripheral neuropathy.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Urinary albumin creatinine ratio | 35 mg/mmol | |
| eGFR creatinine | 47 ml/min/1.73m² (eGFR creatinine of 64 ml/min/1.73 m² during previous clinic visit 6 months before) | |
| HbA1c | 50 mmol/mol | |
| K | 5.1 mmol/L | 3.5–5.5 |
| Urea | 10.5 mg/dL | 7–20 |
| Creatinine | 96 µmol/L | 60–115 |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in her further management?**
explanation_md:
The significant decline in eGFR creatinine for this patient is suggestive of progression of CKD (diabetic nephropathy) which warrants a referral to the renal clinic.

According to NICE guidelines, progression of CKD is defined by the presence of:

- A sustained decrease in GFR of ≥25%
- A change in GFR category within 12 months
- A sustained decrease in GFR of ≥15 ml/min/1.73 m² per year

In addition to CKD progression, referral to the renal clinic should be considered if:

- GFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m² (GFR category G4 or G5) with or without diabetes
- ACR ≥70 mg/mmol (unless known to be caused by diabetes and appropriately treated)
- ACR ≥30 mg/mmol (ACR category A3) together with haematuria

In patients with CKD and diabetes, aim to keep systolic blood pressure (BP) <130 mm of Hg and diastolic BP <80 mm of Hg. Renin-angiotensin antagonists are preferred agents for BP control in such patients in the presence of microalbuminuria. Stop renin-angiotensin antagonists if serum potassium levels increase to >6 mmol/L and other medications which can lead to hyperkalaemia have been discontinued.

SGLT2 inhibitors have been shown to have a beneficial effect in preventing progression of diabetic nephropathy.

A 25-year-old woman with Type 1 DM (diagnosed when she was 6 years old) was reviewed in the clinic during an annual follow-up visit. She was on basal-bolus insulin regimen (insulin degludec 6 units once a day and insulin novorapid as per carbohydrate counting). She had recently heard about the Free Style Libre flash glucose monitoring system and enquired about her eligibility for funding on the NHS for such a system.

**Which of the following is a criterion for NHS England reimbursement for flash glucose monitoring?**
explanation_md:
Criteria for NHS England flash glucose monitoring reimbursement include:

- People with Type 1 DM (or with any form of diabetes and on insulin treatment) who are clinically indicated as requiring intensive monitoring (>8 times/day)
- Pregnant women with Type 1 DM
- People with Type 1 diabetes who are unable to routinely self-monitor blood glucose due to disability
- Recurrent hypoglycaemic episodes or hypoglycaemic unawareness

The full list of criteria can be found at: https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/national-arrangements-for-funding-of-relevant-diabetes-patients-v1.2.pdf

A 19-year-old university student with Type 1 DM was reviewed in the adolescent diabetes clinic. She had been on meal-time aspart insulin injections (tds, dose based on carbohydrate counting), with a basal injection of glargine insulin at night-time. Her home blood glucose readings were variable, ranging from 5 to 15 mmol/L, and her HbA1c readings were 75 mmol/mol (9%).

**According to NICE guidelines, which one of the following is the correct HbA1c cut-off recommended for the use of continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (insulin pump) in adults and children over the age of 12 years with Type 1 DM?**
explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines, insulin pump therapy should be considered in adults and children >12 years of age with Type 1 diabetes if:

- Attempts to reach target HbA1c with multiple insulin injections is leading to disabling hypoglycaemic episodes *or*
- HbA1c levels >8.5%, despite multiple daily insulin injections

A 65-year-old man was admitted to the medical assessment unit with generalized lethargy, nausea, and malaise. He had a background history of Type 2 DM and end-stage renal failure, and was waiting to begin haemodialysis therapy. He was oliguric on admission. On examination, he was clinically dehydrated, his blood pressure was 150/60 mmHg, and he had a pulse rate of 70 beats/minute. His systemic examination was unremarkable.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 106 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 6.0 mmol/L | 3.5–5.5 |
| Urea | 30 mg/dL | 5–9 |
| Creatinine | 565 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| FT4 | 15.5 pmol/L | 9–19.1 |
| TSH | 0.55 mU/L | 0.35–5.00 |
| Serum osmolality | 292 mOsmol/kg | 275–295 |
| Urine osmolality | 502 mOsmol/kg | |
| Urine sodium | <20 mmol/L | |

**Which one of the following is the correct management approach for this patient?**
explanation_md:
The serum osmolality in this patient is 292 mOsmol/kg, despite having low sodium of 106 mmol/L, suggestive of high blood glucose values:

- Serum osmolality: 2 × Na + urea + glucose
- 292 mOsmol/kg = 2 × 106 + 30 + glucose
- 292 mOsmol/kg = 212 + 30 + glucose
- 292 mOsmol/kg = 242 + glucose
- Glucose = 292–242 = 50 mmol/L

The correct management approach for this patient is to start intravenous fluids and insulin infusion as he is clinically dehydrated with elevated blood glucose levels, caused by having translocational hyponatraemia.

A 70-year-old woman was admitted to the accident and emergency unit with sudden-onset severe headache and nausea. She had a background history of hypertension, osteoarthritis, and dyslipidaemia. She was taking amlodipine, atorvastatin, and paracetamol tablets. On examination, she had an elevated blood pressure of 190/104 mmHg, a Glasgow coma score (GCS) of 15/15, with normal systemic examination and no focal neurological deficit.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 129 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 5.5 mmol/L | 3.5–5.5 |
| Urea | 10 mg/dL | 5–9 |
| Creatinine | 125 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| FT4 | 6.5 pmol/L | 9–19.1 |
| TSH | 0.12 mU/L | 0.35–5.00 |
| Serum osmolality | 280 mOsmol/kg | 275–295 |
| Urine osmolality | 442 mOsmol/kg | |
| Urine sodium | 24 mmol/L | |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?**
explanation_md: This woman has secondary hypothyroidism in view of her biochemical results of low FT4 and inappropriately low normal TSH. She has presented with sudden onset of headache and nausea, and pituitary apoplexy should be considered as a diagnosis. Pituitary apoplexy may occur on a background of expansion of a pre-existing pituitary adenoma, which may or may not have been diagnosed previously. The features of sudden-onset headache and ophthalmoplegia (third, fourth, and sixth nerve palsies) should alert to the possibility of pituitary apoplexy. The initiation of steroids in these settings may be life-saving. It is a differential diagnosis of angiographically negative subarachnoid haemorrhage.

An 88-year-old man was admitted to the medical assessment unit with a history of recurrent falls and progressive confusion. He had a background history of vascular dementia, previous stroke, and dyslipidaemia. He was on ramipril, phenytoin, simvastatin, frusemide, and aspirin therapy.

On examination, his blood pressure was 104/70 mmHg. He had a pulse of 94 beats/minute and a normal systemic examination, with no focal neurological deficit.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 126 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 3.2 mmol/L | 3.5–5.5 |
| Urea | 12.8 mg/dL | 5–9 |
| Creatinine | 91 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| FT4 | 14.4 pmol/L | 9–19.1 |
| TSH | 8.1 mU/L | 0.35–5.00 |
| Serum osmolality | 272 mOsmol/kg | 275–295 |
| Urine osmolality | 402 mOsmol/kg | |
| Urine sodium | 40 mmol/L | |
| Random cortisol | 502 nmol/L | |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate management approach in his case?**
explanation_md: This man has biochemical features of dehydration (elevated urea levels); his low Na level is most probably due to hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, rather than syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). The key point to remember in clinical practice is that the urinary spot sodium test results are influenced by hydration status, as well as medications being taken. In this patient, despite his relative hypovolaemic state, urinary sodium levels are 40 mmol (rather than <10 mmol as expected in a patient with dehydration) due to the concomitant use of diuretic therapy.

explanation_md: This patient has euvolaemic hyponatraemia, and her biochemical results are consistent with a diagnosis of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis. The vasopressin secretion in patients with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis is inappropriate as it occurs independently of effective serum osmolality or circulating volume. In a patient with acute hyponatraemia due to the syndrome of inappropriate diuresis, 3% saline needs to be used in the presence of red-flag features such as encephalopathic seizures (due to low Na), coma, reduced Glasgow coma score (GCS), or vomiting.

Investigations:

| HbA1c | 50 mmol/mol | <46 |
| Urine albumin creatinine ratio | >300 mg/mmol | |

**Which one of the following is suggestive of an alternative aetiology for the renal impairment, rather than development of diabetic nephropathy?**

options.A: Absence of active sediment in urine

explanation_md:
The presence of the following clinical and biochemical characteristics should prompt a search for an alternative aetiology for renal impairment in patients with diabetes:

- Duration of Type 2 DM <5 years and Type 1 DM <10 years
- Absence of diabetic retinopathy
- Presence of active sediment in urine
- Rapid decline in eGFR
- Refractory hypertension (although systemic hypertension is common)
- Massive albuminuria
- >30% decline in eGFR within 2–3 months of initiation of ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy
- Significant haematuria
- Presence of systemic illness

**Foot X-rays should ideally be done when weight bearing (if possible).** Dorsal-planter and oblique views are commonly used to visualize the foot bones. Use a systematic approach to review foot X-rays.

stem_md:
A 52-year-old man presented to the diabetes clinic with an 8-month history of excruciating pain in his feet, which was keeping him awake in the night. He had been on pregabalin tablets (300 mg twice a day) for pain relief for over 6 months, although he did not feel it to be beneficial for symptom control. He was diagnosed as having Type 1 diabetes in his early 20s and had been on a basal-bolus insulin regimen (short-acting human insulin with meals, with a glargine insulin injection in the evening). On examination, he had bilateral pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy changes, with reduced vibration, as well as pin-prick sensation (as checked by monofilament) in the feet.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Urea | 22.0 mg/dL | 7–20 |
| Creatinine | 122 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| eGFR | 68 mL/minute/1.73 m² | |
| HbA1c | 79 mmol/mol | <46 |

**According to NICE guidelines (CG173), which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment option for this patient in view of ongoing neuropathic pain?**

options.B: Reduce pregabalin tablet dose and add tramadol

explanation_md:
**According to NICE guidelines, you can offer a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin as initial treatment for neuropathic pain (except for trigeminal neuralgia, where carbamazepine is the initial choice).** If the initial treatment is not effective or is not tolerated, offer one of the remaining three drugs, and consider switching again if the second and third drugs tried are also not effective or not tolerated. Moreover, you can consider tramadol only if acute rescue therapy is needed, while topical capsaicin cream can be used for people with localized neuropathic pain who wish to avoid, or who cannot tolerate, oral treatments.

In this patient, as pregabalin tablets have been ineffective to control neuropathic pain, amitriptyline (or duloxetine) can be started, with gradual tapering of the pregabalin tablet dose (stop pregabalin tablets over 1–2 weeks).

stem_md:
A 16-year-old girl presented to her GP with an 8-week history of increased thirst, weight loss, and increased frequency of micturition. She had no previous history of any medical illness. On examination, she had mild dehydration and her systemic examination was normal.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 133 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 3.6 mmol/L | 3.5–5.5 |
| Urea | 8.5 mg/dL | 5–9 |
| Creatinine | 110 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| Random glucose | 18.5 mmol/L | |
| Urine albumin: creatinine ratio | <3 mg/mmol | |

A clinical diagnosis of Type 1 DM was made, based on her osmotic symptoms with elevated blood glucose levels. She was started on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. During a follow-up visit, she was asymptomatic and clinically well. Her home blood glucose levels were in the target range (4–7 mmol/L: fasting/pre-meal and 5–9 mmol/L: post-meal).

**According to NICE guidelines (NG18), which of the following should be offered for monitoring during her follow-up visits to the diabetes clinic?**
explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines, children and young people with Type 1 diabetes should be offered screening for:

- Thyroid disease, at diagnosis and annually thereafter, until transfer to adult services
- Diabetic retinopathy, annually from 12 years old
- Moderately increased albuminuria (albumin to creatinine ratio [ACR] 3–30 mg/mmol; ‘microalbuminuria’) to detect diabetic kidney disease, annually from 12 years old
- Hypertension, annually from 12 years

It is important to be aware of the following relatively rare complications associated with Type 1 diabetes:

- Addison’s disease
- Coeliac disease
- Juvenile cataracts
- Necrobiosis lipoidica
