A 25-year-old man of South East Asian origin was incidentally detected to have an elevated random blood glucose level of 15 mmol/L, while he underwent routine blood tests. He had no previous history of medical illness and was not on any regular medications. He had a strong family history of diabetes. On examination, his BMI was 24.5 kg/m². His general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 135 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 4.5 mmol/L | 3.5–5.5 |
| Urea | 7.5 mg/dL | 5–9 |
| Creatinine | 90 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| Fasting glucose | 12.5 mmol/L | |
| HbA1c | 103 mmol/mol | <46 |
| Serum ketones | 3.1 mmol/L | |

**The presence of which one of the following clinical/biochemical features is suggestive of a diagnosis of Type 1 diabetes in his case?**
explanation_md:
In a patient who appears to have Type 2 diabetes, consider a diagnosis of Type 1 diabetes if he/she has:

- Ketonaemia
- Marked weight loss
- No features of metabolic syndrome

Similarly, consider a diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes/monogenic diabetes in younger adults if:

- Normal body weight in the presence of a strong family history or diabetes diagnosed aged <1 year (s/o monogenic diabetes)
- Family history of diabetes with obesity (likely Type 2 diabetes)

South East Asian men are prone to Type 2 DM with a comparatively lower BMI, and measurement of waist circumference is deemed more accurate in this particular ethnic subgroup.

stem_md:
A 54-year-old man was reviewed in the diabetes clinic on a follow-up visit. He had been diagnosed as having Type 2 diabetes around 8 years before and was on metformin, gliclazide, and dapagliflozin tablets. His glycaemic control was suboptimal, as reflected by elevated home blood glucose readings. On examination, he had a BMI of 26 kg/m². He had bilateral background diabetic retinopathy changes in the eyes.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Urea | 10.5 mg/dL | 5–9 |
| Creatinine | 125 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| Fasting glucose | 7.5 mmol/L | |
| eGFR | 55 mL/minute/ 1.73 m² | |
| HbA1c | 70 mmol/mol | <46 |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in his management, based on NICE guidelines (NG28)?**
explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines, insulin-based therapies should be considered as a second intensification when HbA1c remains suboptimal (>58 mmol/L) despite using two or more oral anti-diabetic agents.

- Human NPH insulin injected at bedtime or bd remains the initial recommended insulin.
- A long-acting insulin analogue (insulin detemir or glargine) can be considered if:
  - the patient needs assistance from a carer or healthcare professional to inject insulin to reduce the frequency of injections; or
  - the patient’s lifestyle is restricted by recurrent symptomatic hypoglycaemic episodes; or
  - the patient cannot use the device to inject NPH insulin.

Pre-mixed (biphasic) human insulin bd can be considered, especially if HbA1c >9.0% (75 mmol/mol).

stem_md:
A 48-year-old man with Type 1 diabetes for over three decades was reviewed in the diabetes clinic. He had been on basal-bolus insulin with suboptimal glycaemic control, as reflected by elevated home blood glucose readings. He had noticed a deterioration in his vision over the previous 4 weeks. On examination, he had evidence of venous loops and exudates within a disc diameter of the centre of the fovea.

**Which of the following are not indications for referral to the ophthalmologist in a patient with diabetic retinopathy?**
explanation_md:
A patient with diabetic retinopathy should be referred to ophthalmology, in accordance with the National Screening Committee criteria and timelines, if any of these features are present:

- Sudden loss of vision
- Rubeosis iridis
- Pre-retinal or vitreous haemorrhage
- Retinal detachment
- Any large sudden unexplained drop in visual acuity

stem_md:
A 55-year-old man with a background history of Type 1 diabetes was reviewed in the diabetes clinic during a routine follow-up visit. He was on a basal-bolus insulin regimen comprising novorapid insulin (3 times a day, along with meals) and degludec insulin (night-time). He had recently undergone annual retinal screening and was graded as having R1M0 changes bilaterally.

**Which of the following findings can be seen in his retinal images?**
explanation_md: R1MO is the grade given to background diabetic retinopathy. In the case of this patient, annual screening is recommended and there is no need for referral to ophthalmology. The NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme aims to reduce the risk of sight loss by the early detection and treatment, if needed, of diabetic retinopathy and maculopathy. Research has shown that screening could prevent sight loss in more than 400 people with diabetes per year.

stem_md:
A 58-year-old male with a known history of Type 2 diabetes reported symptoms of fever, headache, and mild cough for 3 days. He was taking metformin (500 mg twice a day) and empagliflozin (10 mg once a day) tablets for blood glucose control. A Reverse transcription Polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) test confirmed the diagnosis of COVID-19 infection. He was advised to stay home, with monitoring of oxygen saturation using a pulse oximeter. After 1 week, he presented to the hospital with worsening shortness of breath and oxygen saturation in room air <92%. His chest X-ray showed ground-glass patchy pneumonic changes. He was admitted for oxygen and dexamethasone therapy. During admission, he was noticed to have a blood glucose level of 20 mmol/L on two occasions and serum ketone levels <1mmol/L.

**Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for his further management?**

options.A: Give correction dose of rapid-acting insulin

explanation_md:
According to the COncise adVice on Inpatient Diabetes (COVID: Diabetes), all patients with diabetes and COVID-19 infection should have their blood glucose and capillary ketones measured initially. If their glucose is >12 mmol/L, it is very important to have further investigations to rule out any diabetic emergencies, such as DKA or a hyperosmolar hypercglycaemic state (HHS). Metformin and empagliflozin need to be stopped in view of an acute illness.

If DKA/HHS is excluded, and the patient has not received any insulin in the previous 4 hours (insulin naïve patient or on oral medications), correction doses of rapid-acting insulin can be given. If the patient requires more than two corrective doses within 24 hours, intermediate or long-acting insulin can be initiated and adjusted accordingly.

stem_md:
A 41-year-old man was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with a diagnosis of severe COVID-19 pneumonitis. He had been previously well and was not on any medications prior to this admission. He required non-invasive ventilation to maintain oxygen saturation while in the ICU. He was also started on dexamethasone 6 mg IV once daily. He was noticed to have a morning glucose reading of 18 mmol/L.

**With regards to dexamethasone-induced hyperglycaemia in COVID-19 patients, which of the following statements is correct?**

options.A: Basal insulin injection is unsafe in view of the risk of hypoglycaemia
options.B: Intermediate-acting insulin is not recommended in acute settings
options.C: Patients with no history of diabetes are unlikely to suffer from ketoacidosis
options.E: Target blood glucose readings are 4–8 mmol/L

explanation_md:
Dexamethasone reduces mortality in people with COVID-19 who require ventilation or oxygen therapy, as per the findings from the RECOVERY trial. Corticosteroid therapy is associated with impaired glucose metabolism and predisposes to HHS in vulnerable individuals. COVID-19 infection has been reported to be associated with increased insulin resistance and impaired insulin secretion, resulting in hyperglycaemia and precipitation of DKA in individuals who may or may not have diabetes.

The COncise adVice on Inpatient Diabetes group has produced guidance on the management of blood glucose in patients with COVID-19 and dexamethasone-induced hyperglycaemia. According to these guidelines:

- The target blood glucose (BG) is 6–10 mmol/L (up to 12 mmol/L is acceptable).
- Check the BG at least 6-hourly (or more frequently if BG readings are not in the target range).
- Exclude Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic syndrome (HHS) (check ketones, BG, venous pH, HCO3, U & E)

While sulphonylureas (SU) can be used to counteract steroid-induced hyperglycaemia, SUs are NOT recommended in the context of COVID-19 infection as β-cell function may be impaired and insulin resistance is likely to be severe. For this reason, these recommendations differ from those in the JBDS guidelines on the management of hyperglycaemia and steroid (glucocorticoid) therapy.

stem_md:
A 66-year-old woman was admitted to hospital with severe central chest pain radiating to the left arm. The pain was worse on exertion and relieved with nitroglycerin spray. She had a past medical history of Type 2 DM for which she was on metformin therapy (1 g twice a day). On examination, her BMI was 32 kg/m². She had central obesity, although there was no proximal myopathy or easy bruisability.

The electrocardiogram (ECG) on admission showed ST-segment depression in the lateral leads (V3–V6). A subsequent angiogram confirmed the presence of coronary artery disease for which she underwent successful angioplasty. An echocardiogram on admission showed normal left ventricular function. She was initiated on β-blockers, atorvastatin, and dual anti-platelet therapy. You were asked for advice with regards to her blood glucose control.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| HbA1c | 68 mmol/mol | |
| eGFR | 82 ml/min/1.73 m² | |
| Urine albumin: creatinine ratio | <3 mg/mmol creatinine | |

**Which one of the following is considered as the most appropriate second-line therapy (along with metformin) for this patient, based on the American Diabetes Association (ADA)/European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) 2018 consensus report on the management of hyperglycaemia in Type 2 DM?**
explanation_md:
The consensus report by the ADA/EASD for the management of hyperglycaemia in Type 2 DM (published in 2018) recommends an assessment for the presence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), heart failure, and CKD to decide the most appropriate second-line therapy along with metformin (which remains the first-line therapy). This was based on the evidence derived from several landmark cardiovascular outcome trials (CVOTs)—namely, LEADER, SUSTAIN-6, REWIND for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) and EMPA-REG, DECLARE- TIMI 58, and CANVAS for sodium glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i).

The ADA/EASD consensus recommends the addition of GLP-1 RA for patients with established ASCVD, as in the given clinical scenario. In the presence of heart failure and/or chronic kidney disease, SGLT2i are the preferred therapeutic agents.

Liraglutide, subcutaneous semaglutide, albiglutide, and dulaglutide have been shown to be associated with a reduction in composite cardiovascular outcomes. Lixisenatide, weekly exenatide, and oral semaglutide have been shown to be non-inferior (although not associated with superiority) as far as a reduction of composite cardiovascular outcomes is concerned.

stem_md:
A 70-year-old man was admitted to hospital with progressive shortness of breath which had limited his day-to-day activity. He had woken up in the night with severe shortness of breath, with symptoms worsened on lying down flat. He had a background history of Type 2 DM for over 10 years. He was on metformin and saxagliptin tablets prior to hospital admission. On examination, his BMI was 30 kg/m². He had pedal oedema and jugular venous pressure was raised. He had bilateral reduced air entry on lung-base auscultation. Chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly, bilateral pleural effusion, and pulmonary congestion.

He was treated on the lines of congestive cardiac failure and started on diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and β blockers as per the recommendation from the cardiology team. He responded well to the therapy and was deemed fit for discharge after 5 days in hospital. You were asked to review his glucose-lowering medication regimen prior to discharge from hospital.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| HbA1c | 58 mmol/L | |
| eGFR | 62 mL/minute/1.73 m² | |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate management plan for him?**

options.B: Stop metformin and add GLP1 RA
options.C: Stop saxagliptin and add GLP1 RA
options.D: Stop saxagliptin and add SGLT2 inhibitor

explanation_md:
SGLT2 inhibitors remain the preferred glucose-lowering agents in Type 2 DM patients with a background of heart failure. Saxagliptin needs to be stopped for the patient in this scenario as its use is associated with an increased risk of hospitalization for heart failure based on the results of the SAVOR-TIMI 53 clinical trial published in 2013. Multicentric randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with alogliptin (EXAMINE), sitagliptin (TECOS), and linagliptin (CAROLINA and CARMELINA) have shown these agents to be non-inferior to placebo as far cardiovascular outcomes are concerned.

Based on evidence derived from the EMPA-REG (Empagliflozin Cardiovascular Outcome Event Trial in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Patients), CANVAS program (Canagliflozin Cardiovascular Assessment Study), and DECLARE-TIMI 58 trial (Dapagliflozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events–Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 58), SGLT2i use has been observed to reduce the risk of heart failure (HF) events. Dapagliflozin use in patients with established heart failure (DAPA-HF trial) showed a reduction in the risk of worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes, even in patients with no history of diabetes.

stem_md:
A 16-year-old boy was reviewed in the joint paediatric/young adolescent diabetes transition clinic. He had a background history of obesity, insulin resistance, and Type 2 DM. He had suffered from poor vision since birth and had had worsening hearing since he was 10 years old. On examination, he had pedal oedema, raised jugular venous pressure, and bilateral reduced air entry on lung-base auscultation.

**Which one of the following is the correct diagnosis?**
explanation_md:
Alstrom syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterized by vision and hearing abnormalities, obesity in childhood, insulin resistance, DM, heart disease (dilated cardiomyopathy), and slowly progressive kidney (renal) dysfunction, potentially leading to renal failure. It is due to mutations in the *ALMS1* gene. There is no specific treatment for this disease apart from managing symptoms and complications.

Table 6.4 sums up the genetic conditions/syndromes associated with diabetes.

**Table 6.4** Genetic conditions/syndromes associated with diabetes

| Condition | Genetic defect | Comments |
|---|---|---|
| Transient neonatal diabetes (TND) | Chromosome 6q24 imprinting abnormalities | Neonates present with growth delay and diabetes within the first week of life; remission is expected at 3 months of age, though there might be a tendency to develop diabetes later in life |
| Developmental delay, epilepsy, and neonatal diabetes (DEND) syndrome | KCNJ11 and ABCC8 related K-ATP channel gene mutations | DEND is the most severe form of permeant neonatal diabetes |
| Alstrom syndrome | Rare autosomal recessive disease due to ALMS1 gene mutation | Early-onset truncal obesity, insulin resistance, and Type 2 diabetes; cone-rode dystrophy; hearing loss; cardiomyopathy |
| Wolfram syndrome | WFS1 gene linked to chromosome 4p | Characterized by diabetes insipidus, diabetes (non-autoimmune), optic atrophy, and deafness (a set of conditions referred to as DIDMOAD). |

stem_md:
A 42-year-old schoolteacher was reviewed in the diabetes clinic during an annual review visit. He had been diagnosed with Type 1 DM 15 years before. He was on a basal-bolus insulin regimen comprising glargine (20 units at night) and novorapid (4 units before meals). He had a family history of cardiovascular disease (a first cousin had had a myocardial infarction at the age of 45 years). He was concerned about the risk of having a heart attack given his raised total cholesterol levels.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 143 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 4.2 mmol/L | 3.5–5.5 |
| Urea | 19 mg/dL | 7–20 |
| Creatinine | 99 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| eGFR | >90 mL/minute/1.73 m² | |
| HbA1c | 66 mmol/mol | <48 |
| Total cholesterol | 5.4 mmol/L | <4 |

**According to NICE guidelines (CG181), which one of the following is a recommended indication for starting statin therapy for primary prevention in people with Type 1 DM?**

options.C: Family history of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in first-degree relatives

explanation_md:
According to NICE guidelines, statin therapy can be offered to adults with Type 1 DM if:

- Older than 40 years
- Diabetes duration >10 years
- Established nephropathy
- In presence of other risk factors for CVD

In people with Type 2 DM, atorvastatin 20 mg can be offered for primary prevention if the 10-year risk of developing CVD based on QRISK2 assessment tool is ≥10%.

stem_md:
A 53-year-old man was admitted to hospital with community acquired pneumonia. He had a background history of Type 1 DM for over 30 years. His pre-admission insulin regimen included glargine (34 units before bed) and lispro (6 units before each meal). He complained of productive cough, nausea, and reduced appetite. On day 2 (post admission), he felt sweaty and clammy. His capillary blood glucose was recorded as 2.6 mmol/L. He was conscious, although complained of mild headache.

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate management step?**
explanation_md:
According to the Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care (JBDS-IP) Group guidelines for the management of hypoglycaemia in adults with DM, the treatment of hypoglycaemia in a conscious adult patient in hospital should be with 15–20 g of quick-acting carbohydrate, such as 5–7 tablets of Dextrosol®, 4 or 5 Glucotabs®, or 150–200 ml of pure fruit juice (e.g. orange). Since the introduction of the UK government sugar tax in 2018, Lucozade®—which was commonly used to treat hypoglycaemia—is no longer recommended due to the quantities required to achieve 15–20 g carbohydrate (and the variation in carbohydrate content between different types of Lucozade®).

Once the hypoglycaemia is treated (blood glucose >4.0 mmol/L) and the patient has recovered, give a long-acting carbohydrate of the patient’s choice: for example, two biscuits, one slice of bread/toast, 200–300 ml of milk (not soya), or normal meal if it is due (must contain carbohydrate). In patients with moderately severe hypoglycaemia (e.g. patient is unable to take oral carbohydrate and/or are agitated), who are able to swallow, give either 1.5 –2 tubes 40% glucose gel (Glucogel®) squeezed into the mouth between the teeth and gums. This can be repeated up to three times if blood glucose remains <4 mmol/L. In patients with severe hypoglycaemia (unconscious, fitting, or having persistent hypoglycaemia), give intravenous dextrose (200 ml of 10% dextrose or 100 ml of 20% dextrose over 15 minutes) or intramuscular glucagon (1 mg).

stem_md:
A 72-year-old woman with a right knee anterior cruciate ligament tear was awaiting an elective laparoscopic ligament reconstruction. She had a background history of Type 2 DM diagnosed 6-years before. She was on metformin (1 g twice daily), sitagliptin (50 mg once daily), and glargine (20 units once daily). Her elective surgical procedure was booked for 8.30 a.m. and she was expected to miss only one meal during the day.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| HbA1c | 65 mmol/L | |
| eGFR | 90 mL/minute/1.73 m² | |

**Which one of the following is the correct management approach for peri-operative management of her diabetes?**
explanation_md:
According to the Joint British Diabetes Societies (JBDS) guidelines for the management of adults with diabetes undergoing surgery:

- If HbA1c is >69 mmol/mol prior to the surgery, glucose lowering therapy needs to be optimised.
- Target capillary glucose readings are 6–12 mmol/L (peri-operative period)
- Consider reducing basal insulin dose by 20% a day prior to surgery

Metformin need not be stopped for the patient in this scenario, and variable-rate insulin infusion is not needed in her case as there is no risk of prolonged starvation (only one missed meal).

stem_md:
A 68-year-old man was admitted to hospital for an elective repair of a left-sided inguinal hernia. He was known to have had Type 1 DM for over 30 years. He was on a basal bolus insulin regimen comprising glargine (12 units in the morning) and novorapid (6 units before each meal). His operation was scheduled for 9.00 a.m. in the morning and it was anticipated that he might have to miss only one meal during the day.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| HbA1c | 60 mmol/L | |
| eGFR | 58 mL/minute/1.73 m² | |

**Which one of the following is correct advice related to insulin therapy titration during the peri-operative period?**

options.A: Half the dose of long-acting insulin (on day of surgery)
options.B: Half the dose of short-acting insulin (till he resumes eating and drinking normally)
options.C: Omit long-acting insulin on day of surgery
options.D: Omit short-acting insulin (till he resumes eating and drinking normally)
options.E: Switch to pre-mix insulin (twice a day)

explanation_md: Long-acting insulin should not be stopped for this patient (even if the patient is on variable-rate insulin) as this may lead to rebound hyperglycaemia. The most sensible approach would be to reduce the morning dose of the long-acting insulin (usually by 20%) and omit the short-acting insulin in the morning (if breakfast is missed). Resume short-acting insulin only when the patient resumes eating and drinking normally.

stem_md:
A 70-year-old man was admitted to hospital after suffering from an acute-onset cerebrovascular accident (haemorrhagic stroke). He subsequently developed aspiration pneumonia and continued to deteriorate clinically while in the stroke unit. He had a background history of Type 1 DM and was on glargine (20 units at night) and novorapid (6 units before meals). As his clinical condition continued to deteriorate despite best possible medical measures, the admitting team decided that his need was for an end-of-life care pathway.

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate management approach in his case?**

options.A: Give glargine in the morning and stop short-acting insulin
options.B: Give stat doses of short-acting insulin if blood glucose >15 mmol/L
options.C: Stop basal-bolus insulin and monitor blood glucose every 6 hours
options.D: Stop glargine and continue with short-acting insulin

explanation_md: At the end of life, the emphasis should be on ensuring the patient is comfortable and pain-free. Frequent monitoring of blood glucose and use of short-acting insulin is not justified. It is equally important to prevent any physical distress caused by extremes of blood glucose readings. In patients with Type 1 DM, once-daily long-acting insulin (preferably injected in the morning) with a once-daily check of blood glucose at 6.00 p.m. is recommended

stem_md:
A 25-year-old woman was admitted to hospital with repeated vomiting and abdominal pain. She had a background history of Type 1 DM (diagnosed when she was aged 8 years). She was on a basal-bolus insulin regimen comprising degludec (10 units at night-time) with pre-meal short-acting insulin (dose based on carbohydrate counting). On examination, she was dehydrated. Her respiratory rate was 26/minute and she had blood pressure of 110/60 mm of Hg. Systemic examination was normal. She was diagnosed as having diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in the accident and emergency (A&E) department, and she was initiated on treatment based on DKA management national guidelines.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Haemoglobin | 138 g/L | 130–160 |
| Serum sodium | 140 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| Serum potassium | 2.9 mmol/L | 3.5–4.5 |
| eGFR | 52 ml/minute/1.73 m² | |
| Venous pH | 7.14 | 7.35–7.45 |
| Venous HCO3 | 12 meq/L | 20–29 |
| Blood ketones | 4.8 mmol/L | |
| Blood glucose | 23 mmol/L | |
| HbA1c | 94 mmol/mol | <48 mmol/mol |

As you are the medical registrar on call, you are asked by the A & E department’s house officer to accept the patient’s transfer to the medical ward for further management. **The presence of which of the following findings would indicate a need for a referral to the high-dependency unit (HDU)?**
explanation_md:
According to the JBDS guidelines for the management of DKA in adults, the presence of one or more of the following may indicate severe DKA:

- Blood ketones >6mmol/L
- Bicarbonate level <5mmol/L
- Venous/arterial pH <7.0
- Hypokalaemia on admission (<3.5mmol/L)
- GCS <12 or abnormal AVPU scale
- Oxygen saturation <92% on air, systolic BP < 90 mmHg, pulse >100 or <60 beats/minute
- Anion gap >16

The presence of any of these signs should trigger a consultant physician review and a referral to Level 2/HDU. In this patient, her potassium levels are extremely low and might drop further on initiation of fixed-rate insulin infusion. Meticulous fluid replacement with additional potassium replacement might be needed and be deemed safer in the HDU.

stem_md:
An 80-year-old woman was admitted to the acute medical admission unit as she had been feeling generally unwell for a week. She had a past medical history of hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and Type 2 DM. Her medications included metformin (1 g twice daily), sitagliptin (100 mg once daily), and amlodipine (10 mg once daily). On admission, she was confused and dehydrated. Her blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg and her heart rate was 119 beats/minute. She had coarse inspiratory crepitations on auscultation of the right lung base.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Haemoglobin | 102 g/L | 130–160 |
| Serum sodium | 165 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| Serum potassium | 4.2 mmol/L | 3.5–4.5 |
| Urea | 25.5 mmol/L | 2.5–7 |
| Creatinine | 172 umol/L | 50–120 |
| eGFR | 23 ml/minute/1.73 m² | |
| Venous pH | 7.32 | 7.35–7.45 |
| Venous HCO3 | 18 meq/L | 20–29 |
| Blood ketones | 0.6 mmol/L | |
| Blood glucose | 42 mmol/L | |
| HbA1c | 85 mmol/mol | <48 mmol/mol |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial fluid therapy for her?**

options.C: Fixed-rate insulin infusion at a rate of 0.1 U/kg/hr
options.D: Fixed-rate insulin infusion at a rate of 0.05 U/kg/hr

explanation_md:
This patient fulfils the diagnostic criteria of HSS. This is based on the presence of hypovolaemia, significant hyperglycaemia (laboratory glucose >30 mmol/L), without significant capillary ketones (<3 mmol/L and osmolarity of >320 mosmol/kg). HHS carries a higher mortality risk than DKA, which can reach up to 20%. Fluid losses in HHS are estimated to be 100–220 ml/kg (6–13 litres in a person weighing 60 kg and 10–22 litres in a person weighing 100 kg). Extreme caution is needed with regards to the rate of fluid therapy, especially in the elderly, as very rapid rehydration may cause fluid overload and acute pulmonary oedema.

In HHS, the JBDS recommend the use of 0.9% sodium chloride as the principle fluid to treat hypovolaemia. The use of 0.45% sodium chloride might be considered if the osmolality is not declining despite adequate positive fluid balance with the standard sodium chloride infusion. To avoid rapid fluid replacement, it is recommended to aim for a positive balance of 3–6 litres by 12 hours, while the remaining replacement of estimated fluid losses should be replaced over the next 12 hours.

The use of intravenous insulin (0.05 units/kg/hr; this is half the dose recombined for DKA) can be considered if the blood glucose is not falling at the expected rate with intravenous fluids alone or in the presence significant ketonaemia (capillary ketones >1 mmol/L or urine ketones greater than 2+).

A 26-year-old woman was reviewed in the joint antenatal–diabetes clinic. She had a background history of Type 1 DM diagnosed 8 years before. She was on a basal-bolus insulin regimen comprising degludec (14 units at night-time) and novorapid (dose based on carbohydrate counting). She was in the third trimester (33rd week) of pregnancy. Recent serial ultrasound scans had shown accelerated baby growth and evidence of foetal macrosomia. As a result, she was advised to have an elective Caesarean section at the 34th week of her pregnancy. She was keen to understand more about the diabetes care on the day of her planned elective Caesarean section.

**Which one of the following statements is correct regarding care of this women during labour and the post-natal period?**

options.A: Antenatal steroids are contraindicated given the risk of DKA
options.B: Capillary blood glucose should be checked every 2 hours (while on VRIII)
options.C: Capillary blood glucose target should be 6–10 mmol/L
options.D: During breastfeeding, daily caloric intake should be increased
options.E: Long-acting insulin should be stopped in view of the risk of hypoglycaemia

explanation_md:
JBDS guidelines recommend that all women with diabetes during labour should have capillary blood glucose (CBG) testing hourly whilst on variable-rate insulin infusion (VRIII), aiming for a target reading of 4–7 mmol/L. Administration of antenatal steroids is crucial for foetal lung maturity and should be considered for all women at risk for preterm birth, up to 35+6 weeks of gestation. Glycaemic control may deteriorate for up to 72 hours after steroid administration, but this is not a contraindication to steroid therapy.

As breastfeeding and expressing breast milk can both increase the risk of maternal hypoglycaemia, women should be advised to take extra calories (up to 450 per day) when feeding is fully established. This is done by advising the woman to snack (10–15 g carbohydrate) and drink each time they feed or express milk (including night feeds). Indeed, insulin doses may need adjustment based on calorie and carbohydrate intake.

A 22-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department with repeated nausea and vomiting, and increasing drowsiness. He was known to have Type 1 DM, although he had not attended a diabetes clinic appointment for the previous 3 years. On examination, his blood pressure was 100/40 mm of Hg. His pulse rate was 104/minute and he had a respiratory rate of 32/minute. Systemic examination was normal.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Serum sodium | 132 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| Serum potassium | 4.5 mmol/L | 3.5–4.5 |
| Urea | 12.4 mmol/L | 2.5–7 |
| Creatinine | 137 umol/L | 50–120 |
| Venous pH | 7.22 | 7.35–7.45 |
| Venous HCO3 | 16 meq/L | 20–29 |
| Blood ketones | 3.5 mmol/L | |
| Blood glucose | 28 mmol/L | |
| HbA1c | 127 mmol/mol | <48 mmol/mol |

Based on his clinical presentation and investigation results, a diagnosis of DKA was made and he was treated as per the national DKA treatment protocol. He made a gradual recovery and was transferred across to the medical ward on resolution of DKA, on a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRIII). He remembered that he was prescribed glargine and aspart (novorapid), but he could not recall the dose of insulin injection. He admitted suboptimal compliance with insulin injections and had experienced hypoglycaemic episodes frequently on days when he injected his insulin injection (as per prescribed dose). In the previous 6 hours, he had received 6 units of insulin through the VRIII. His body weight was 60 kg.

**As you are considering switching him from VRIII back to subcutaneous (SC) insulin, what is the estimated dose of glargine for him?**
explanation_md:
There are two methods to calculate the total daily dose (TDD) of insulin:

**1. Weight method: TDD = body weight (kg) × (0.3–0.5).** As this patient reported frequent hypoglycaemia, it is safer to start with a lower dose and titrate accordingly. In this patient, TDD is 18 units (weight is 60 kg). After calculating the TDD, half the TDD will be given as basal and the other half will be divided to pre-meal boluses. In this patient, 9 units will be given as basal glargine, while the remaining 9 units are to be divided into 3 units of insulin novorapid before meals.

**2. VRIII method: An estimate of the daily insulin requirement can be made from the last 6 hours of the VRIII as follows:**

a) Divide the total dose of insulin administered in the last 6 hours of the VRIII by 6 to calculate the average hourly dose of insulin.

b) Multiply this by 20 (not 24, to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia) to estimate the patient’s total daily insulin requirement.

c) A further correction may be needed in some patients, depending on individual insulin sensitivity, previous degree of glycaemic control, and severity of intercurrent illness.

The patient in this scenario has had 6 units of insulin through VRIII in the previous 6 hours. This means that his TDD of insulin is 20 units (remember, as he has risk of hypoglycaemia, we have opted not to give 24 units). Hence, half the TDD (half of 20 = 10) will be given as basal insulin glargine, and the remaining 10 units will be divided as pre-meal boluses (for example, 4 units in the morning, 3 units in the afternoon, 3 units in the evening).

A 62-year-old woman was admitted to the HDU after suffering from a left-sided total anterior circulation stroke. She was known to have Type 2 DM and prior to admission was on pre-mixed insulin (humulin M3, 30 units twice daily). She was reviewed by the speech and language therapist and was deemed unsafe for oral feeding. The team decided to insert a nasogastric tube for the purpose of feeding. You were asked to see her to review her insulin regimen. The dietician was aiming to provide the following diet regimen:

Carbohydrate content of feed = 15 g/100 ml
Intended infusion rate of enteral feed = 100 ml/hour
Intended duration of feed = 16 hours/day

**What is the estimated humulin M3 dose from carbohydrate feed content that she should be given?**
explanation_md:
Before we can attempt to calculate the initial insulin requirement for patients starting on enteral feeding, a few points and calculations must first be taken into account:

a) Total carbohydrate intake from enteral feed: that is the total carbohydrate intake expected from the enteral feed over the duration of feeding (e.g. 16, 20, 24 hours). This is calculated as:

[infusion rate (ml/hour)] × [carbohydrate content (g/100 ml)] × [duration of feeding] ÷ 100

b) Carbohydrate-to-insulin ratio (CIR): this is how many grams of carbohydrate/glucose are covered by 1 unit of insulin. The blood glucose rise from enteral feeds is much more than would occur for normal meals: therefore, 1 unit of insulin will cover less of a carbohydrate load.

- i If not usually on insulin, use a CIR value of 10.
- ii If usual total daily insulin dose (TDID) <40 units, use a value of 8.
- iii If usual TDID >40 units, use a value of 6.

c) Daily nutritional insulin requirement: this is the daily insulin required to cover the enteral feed over the duration of feeding (e.g. 16, 20, 24 hrs). This is calculated as:

**[total carbohydrate intake from feed] ÷ [CIR]**

This number of units is then divided into two doses: the first to be given at the start of the feed and the other given at the midpoint of the feed.

In this patient:

- Carbohydrate content of feed = 15 g/100 ml
- Intended infusion rate of enteral feed = 100 ml/hour
- Intended duration of feed = 16 hours
- She was previously on insulin with TDD >40: therefore CIR = 6
- Total humulin M3 dose = (15 × 100 × 16)/100/6 = 40 units/24 hrs

A 54-year-old woman attended the diabetes clinic for a routine annual check-up. She had been diagnosed as having Type 2 DM about 5 years before. She was also known to have hypertension for which she was taking ramipril (10 mg once daily) and amlodipine (5 mg once daily). On examination, her blood pressure (BP) was 150/80 mmHg. Her recent renal function and urinary albumin creatinine ratio were within the normal range.

**Based on NICE guidelines, what should be the target blood pressure reading for this patient?**
explanation_md: In patients with Type 2 diabetes, NICE recommends a BP target of 140/80 mmHg, while the target for adults with Type 1 diabetes is 135/85 mmHg. A target of 130/80 is recommended by NICE in adults with Type 1 diabetes in the presence of albuminuria or two or more features of metabolic syndromes, and in patients with Type 2 diabetes in the presence of nephropathy, retinopathy, or cerebrovascular disease.

He was otherwise fit and healthy, with no history of any previous medical illness. He was not on any regular medications. His father had Type 2 diabetes and had suffered from a myocardial infarction aged 48 years. On examination, the patient had a BMI of 30 mm/kg² and BP of 130/70 mm of Hg.

Investigations:

| Test | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 140 mmol/L | 135–145 |
| K | 4.3 mmol/L | 3.5–5.5 |
| Urea | 10 mg/dL | 7–20 |
| Creatinine | 100 µmol/L | 60–115 |
| eGFR | >90 mL/minute/1.73 m² | |
| HbA1c | 34 mmol/mol | <48 |
| Total cholesterol | 7.8 mmol/L | <5 |
| Serum triglycerides | 1.2 mmol/L | <4.5 |
| Non-HDL cholesterol | 6.4 mmol/L | <4 |

**Which one of the following is the next step in his management?**

options.A: Calculate QRISK3 score to assess the need for statins
options.B: Refer him to the familial hypercholesterolaemia specialist service

explanation_md: The young patient in this scenario has a clinical diagnosis of possible familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) based on Simon Broome criteria, as he has two readings of total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L and history of premature cardiovascular events in his first-degree relatives. The QRISK3 score should not be used if FH is suspected, but instead, the Simon Broome criteria or the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network Score (DLCNS) are often used to make a clinical diagnosis of FH and assess the need for genetic testing. NICE recommends referring a person to an FH specialist service for DNA testing if they meet the Simon Broome criteria for possible or definite FH, or they have a DLCN score >5.

**Which of the following is the most appropriate management approach based on his clinical presentation?**
